claim: Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) causes 1.5 million deaths a year.
source: Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb), a bacterium that causes 1.5 million deaths a year (Sharma et al., 2006; World Health Organization, 2014), differs from many bacterial pathogens in its infection strategy, which depends on an unusual cell envelope (Cambier et al., 2014).
evidence: Cited from external sources (Sharma et al., 2006; World Health Organization, 2014)

claim: At least a quarter of the genes in the Mtb genome are involved in cell envelope construction and regulation.
source: The importance of this structure is evident from the fact that at least a quarter of the genes in the Mtb genome are involved in its construction and regulation (Doerks et al., 2012).
evidence: Cited from external source (Doerks et al., 2012)

claim: The mycobacterial cell wall consists of peptidoglycan covalently bound to arabinogalactan sugars, which is covalently bound to mycolic acid lipids that make up an outer membrane.
source: The mycobacterial cell wall consists of peptidoglycan (PG) covalently bound to a layer of arabinogalactan sugars, which is in turn covalently bound to a layer of mycolic acid lipids that make up an outer membrane (Alderwick et al., 2015; Cambier et al., 2014).
evidence: Cited from external sources (Alderwick et al., 2015; Cambier et al., 2014)

claim: Regulated cell wall changes are essential for Mtb to cause disease.
source: Regulated cell wall changes are essential for Mtb to cause disease (Doerks et al., 2012; Sharma et al., 2006) and are thought to contribute to phenotypic antibiotic tolerance.
evidence: Cited from external sources (Doerks et al., 2012; Sharma et al., 2006)

claim: TB therapy requires 6–12 months of drug treatment.
source: TB therapy requires 6–12 months of drug treatment.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in the field

claim: The long duration of TB therapy is likely due, in part, to drug tolerance like that observed in stressed, non-growing Mtb cultures.
source: This is likely due, in part, to drug tolerance like that observed in stressed, non-growing Mtb cultures (Wallis et al., 1999).
evidence: Cited from external source (Wallis et al., 1999)

claim: Stressed Mtb exhibits cell wall changes such as thickening, differential staining and chemical alterations.
source: Because stressed Mtb also exhibits cell wall changes such as thickening, differential staining and chemical alterations (Bhamidi et al., 2012; Cunningham and Spreadbury, 1998; Seiler et al., 2003), it seems probable that the cell wall changes contribute to antibiotic tolerance.
evidence: Cited from external sources (Bhamidi et al., 2012; Cunningham and Spreadbury, 1998; Seiler et al., 2003)

claim: Starved, antibiotic tolerant Mtb cells are less permeable to antibiotics.
source: Importantly, starved, antibiotic tolerant Mtb cells have been shown to be less permeable to antibiotics (Sarathy et al., 2013).
evidence: Cited from external source (Sarathy et al., 2013)

claim: The peptidoglycan layer is constructed by transpeptidases and glycosyltransferases, which attach new precursors to the existing cell wall.
source: This layer is constructed by transpeptidases and glycosyltransferases, which attach new precursors to the existing cell wall; and several types of catabolic PG hydrolases, which break bonds in the existing PG.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about peptidoglycan biosynthesis

claim: PG enzymes must be tightly regulated to promote cell growth and septation without compromising wall integrity.
source: PG enzymes must be tightly regulated to promote cell growth and septation without compromising the wall integrity, and to restructure the cell wall to withstand stresses (Kieser and Rubin, 2014).
evidence: Cited from external source (Kieser and Rubin, 2014)

claim: Many PG synthases and hydrolases work together in complexes and regulate each others' enzymatic activity through protein-protein interactions.
source: In addition to the dedicated regulators, many PG synthases and hydrolases work together in complexes and regulate each others' enzymatic activity through protein-protein interactions (Banzhaf et al., 2012; Hett et al., 2010; Smith and Foster, 1995).
evidence: Cited from external sources (Banzhaf et al., 2012; Hett et al., 2010; Smith and Foster, 1995)

claim: Some PG hydrolases have lost their enzymatic activity and function only as regulators.
source: Notably, some PG hydrolases have lost their enzymatic activity and function only as regulators: EnvC in E. coli is missing catalytic residues from its active site but contributes to cell septation by activating the PG amidases AmiA and AmiB (Uehara et al., 2010; Yang et al., 2011).
evidence: Cited from external sources (Uehara et al., 2010; Yang et al., 2011)

claim: cwlM (Rv3915, MSMEG_6935) is predicted to be essential for growth in Mtb.
source: cwlM (Rv3915, MSMEG_6935) is predicted to be essential for growth in Mtb (Zhang et al., 2012), is highly conserved among mycobacteria, and is annotated as an N-acetylmuramoyl-L-alanine amidase of the AmiA/LytC family (hereafter: PG amidase), a type of PG hydrolase.
evidence: Cited from external source (Zhang et al., 2012)

claim: CwlMTB has been shown to have PG amidase activity.
source: CwlMTB has been shown to have PG amidase activity (Deng et al., 2005); however, key residues that coordinate the catalytic Zn2+ are not conserved in CwlM from both Mtb and Msmeg (Yamane et al., 2001) (Figure 1A), implying that it is inefficient as an enzyme.
evidence: Cited from external source (Deng et al., 2005)

claim: Key residues that coordinate the catalytic Zn2+ are not conserved in CwlM from both Mtb and Msmeg.
source: CwlMTB has been shown to have PG amidase activity (Deng et al., 2005); however, key residues that coordinate the catalytic Zn2+ are not conserved in CwlM from both Mtb and Msmeg (Yamane et al., 2001) (Figure 1A), implying that it is inefficient as an enzyme.
evidence: Cited from external source (Yamane et al., 2001) and shown in Figure 1A alignment

claim: Overexpression of CwlM did not affect cell viability.
source: This is supported by our observation that overexpression of CwlM did not affect cell viability (Figure 1—figure supplement 1): overexpression of highly active PG hydrolases usually results in cell lysis (Uehara and Bernhardt, 2011).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: Overexpression of highly active PG hydrolases usually results in cell lysis.
source: This is supported by our observation that overexpression of CwlM did not affect cell viability (Figure 1—figure supplement 1): overexpression of highly active PG hydrolases usually results in cell lysis (Uehara and Bernhardt, 2011).
evidence: Cited from external source (Uehara and Bernhardt, 2011)

claim: Depletion of CwlM by removing Atc results in cell death.
source: Depletion of CwlM by removing Atc results in cell death (Figure 1B).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 1B

claim: CwlM-depleted cells are short, implying a defect in elongation.
source: Microscopy of CwlM-depleted cells shows that they are short, implying a defect in elongation.
evidence: Inferred from microscopy observations

claim: CwlM-depleted cells fail to elongate normally.
source: We found that CwlM-depleted cells fail to elongate normally (Figure 1D,E,F).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 1D, E, F

claim: cwlM E209A D331A is able to complement the WT allele in a growth curve assay.
source: cwlM E209A D331A has zero out of four conserved Zn2+-coordinating residues, but is able to complement the WT allele in a growth curve assay (Figure 1G).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 1G

claim: CwlM is essential for cell survival and elongation in Msmeg, but its presumed amidase active site does not appear to be essential.
source: Thus, CwlM is essential for cell survival and elongation in Msmeg, but its presumed amidase active site does not appear to be essential.
evidence: Inferred from the complementation experiment with amidase-ablated mutant

claim: CwlMTB is phosphorylated at T43 and T382.
source: A proteomic screen in Mtb found that CwlMTB is phosphorylated at T43 and T382 (Prisic et al., 2010).
evidence: Cited from external source (Prisic et al., 2010)

claim: Msmeg CwlM is phosphorylated at T35 and T374, as well as T376 and T378.
source: Mass spectrometry of the gel spots identified phosphorylation at T35 and T374 (equivalent to T43 and T382 in the Mtb protein), as well as T376 and T378, and acetylation at K362 and K369.
evidence: Mass spectrometry data from immunoprecipitated CwlM

claim: Msmeg CwlM is acetylated at K362 and K369.
source: Mass spectrometry of the gel spots identified phosphorylation at T35 and T374 (equivalent to T43 and T382 in the Mtb protein), as well as T376 and T378, and acetylation at K362 and K369.
evidence: Mass spectrometry data from immunoprecipitated CwlM

claim: The L5::cwlM T374A strain grew slowly.
source: Most mutants grew normally but the L5::cwlM T374A strain grew slowly (Figure 2C; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), despite containing normal amounts of CwlM protein (Figure 2D).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A

claim: The L5::cwlM T374A cells were short and defective for polar elongation.
source: The L5::cwlM T374A cells were short (Figure 2E) and defective for polar elongation (Figure 2F).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 2E and 2F

claim: Absence of phosphorylation on T374 inhibits the essential function of CwlM.
source: Because the phenotypes of the L5::cwlM T374A strain are similar to the CwlM depletion (Figure 1), it seems likely that absence of phosphorylation on T374 inhibits the essential function of CwlM, though the T374A mutation could interrupt CwlM function in another way.
evidence: Inferred from similarity of phenotypes between T374A mutant and CwlM depletion

claim: CwlM is a cytoplasmic protein.
source: We measured the accessibility of a cysteine on CwlM to agents with different membrane permeability and found that CwlM is only accessible to agents that can reach the cytoplasm (Figure 2G). Thus, CwlM is a cytoplasmic protein whose essential function is likely activated by phosphorylation.
evidence: Experimental data from SCAM assay shown in Figure 2G

claim: his-MBP-PknBTB(KD) phosphorylates his-CwlMTB more rapidly than other kinases.
source: We found that his-MBP-PknBTB(KD) phosphorylates his-CwlMTB more rapidly than the other kinases (Figure 3A; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Experimental data from phospho-transfer profiling shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B

claim: In vitro, his-MBP-PknBTB phosphorylates his-CwlMTB at threonines 382, 384 and 386.
source: We used mass spectrometry to show that in vitro, his-MBP-PknBTB phosphorylates his-CwlMTB at threonines 382, 384 and 386 (equivalent to T374, 376 and 378 in M. smegmatis, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C

claim: PknBTB overexpression increases CwlM phosphorylation in vivo.
source: We found that PknBTB overexpression increases CwlM phosphorylation.
evidence: Experimental data from immunoprecipitation and western blot

claim: PknB is likely the primary kinase of CwlM.
source: Thus, PknB is likely the primary kinase of CwlM.
evidence: Inferred from in vitro and in vivo phosphorylation data

claim: Three of five suppressor strains contained an identical S368P mutation in the gene murA.
source: Three of five suppressor strains contained an identical S368P mutation in the gene murA.
evidence: Whole genome sequencing data from suppressor screen

claim: MurA is a cytoplasmic enzyme that catalyzes the first dedicated step in PG precursor synthesis.
source: MurA is a cytoplasmic enzyme that catalyzes the first dedicated step in PG precursor synthesis: transfer of an enolpyruvyl group from phosphoenol pyruvate (PEP) onto UDP-N-acetylglucosamine (UDP-GlcNAc) (Marquardt et al., 1992).
evidence: Cited from external source (Marquardt et al., 1992)

claim: The murA S368P allele suppresses the growth defect of the cwlM T374A allele.
source: We found that the cwlM T374A allele and a deletion of the C-terminal tail are poorly tolerated in a WT murA background, but can be recovered at near WT levels in a murA S368P background.
evidence: Experimental data from allele swapping experiments

claim: The entire cwlM gene cannot be deleted in either murA WT or murA S368P background.
source: The entire cwlM gene cannot be deleted in either background (Figure 4B).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 4B

claim: CwlM-FLAG and MurA-strep physically interact.
source: We found that CwlM-FLAG could be precipitated with α-strep beads, but only in the presence of MurA-strep, and vice versa (Figure 4C). Thus, there is a genetic link between cwlM and murA, and the two proteins interact.
evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4C

claim: The reaction rate of his-MurATB is 20–40 times faster in the presence of equimolar his-CwlMTB~P than it is alone or with unphosphorylated his-CwlMTB.
source: We found that the reaction rate of his-MurATB is 20–40 times faster in the presence of equimolar his-CwlMTB~P (Figure 5) than it is alone or with unphosphorylated his-CwlMTB.
evidence: Experimental data from MurA kinetic assays shown in Figure 5

claim: his-CwlMTB with phosphoablative mutations does not appreciably stimulate his-MurATB activity after incubation with his-MBP-PknBTB and ATP.
source: his-CwlMTB with phosphoablative mutations does not appreciably stimulate his-MurATB activity after incubation with his-MBP-PknBTB and ATP (Figure 5E).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 5E

claim: his-CwlMTB alone cannot synthesize EP-UDP-GlcNAc.
source: his-CwlMTB alone cannot synthesize EP-UDP-GlcNAc; MurA is not thought to be phosphorylated (Prisic et al., 2010) and his-MBP-PknBTB cannot stimulate MurA activity in the absence of his-CwlMTB (Figure 5E).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 5E and cited from external source (Prisic et al., 2010)

claim: his-MurATB is maximally activated in a reaction with a 2-fold molar excess of fully phosphorylated his-CwlMTB~P.
source: We measured the stoichiometry of the CwlM:MurA reaction and found that his-MurATB is maximally activated in a reaction with a 2-fold molar excess of fully phosphorylated his-CwlMTB~P (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E,F).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E,F

claim: CwlM~P is a direct activator of MurATB.
source: Thus, CwlM~P activates MurA to initiate PG synthesis. These data with Mtb proteins confirm our model based on the genetic data in Msmeg, and show that CwlMTB~P is a direct activator of MurATB.
evidence: Inferred from biochemical kinetic assays

claim: MurA from other species have much more rapid kinetics and lower Km values than isolated MurATB.
source: MurA from other species have been studied in vitro and shown to have much more rapid kinetics and lower Km values than isolated MurATB (Figure 5B,C; Figure 5—figure supplement 1; Supplementary file 1D [Xu et al., 2014]).
evidence: Comparison with literature data (Xu et al., 2014) and experimental data shown in Figure 5B,C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: CwlM phosphorylation is quickly reduced upon starvation in PBS.
source: We found that CwlM phosphorylation is quickly reduced upon starvation in PBS (Figure 6A).
evidence: Experimental data from immunoprecipitation and western blot shown in Figure 6A

claim: his-MurAMSS368P is more active than the WT protein in all conditions by about 2-fold.
source: We found that his-MurAMSS368P is more active than the WT protein in all conditions by about 2-fold (Figure 6B).
evidence: Experimental data from MurA kinetic assays shown in Figure 6B

claim: The strain carrying murA S368P shows increased fluorescence compared to the WT allele during the first 12 hr of PBS starvation.
source: We observed increased fluorescence in the strain carrying murA S368P as compared to the WT allele during the first 12 hr of PBS starvation, but, by 24 hr, the staining was equivalent between the strains (Figure 6C).
evidence: Experimental data from TADA staining and flow cytometry shown in Figure 6C

claim: Post-translational regulation of MurA is important to control PG metabolism in logarithmic phase growth and during the transition to starvation.
source: We interpret this to mean that post-translational regulation of MurA is important to control PG metabolism in logarithmic phase growth and during the transition to starvation, but that after prolonged starvation other regulatory mechanisms predominate to control PG metabolism.
evidence: Inferred from TADA staining data over time course

claim: There is a 3–100 fold increase in killing of the strain carrying the murA S368P allele when treated with isoniazid, meropenem or rifampin at the initiation of starvation.
source: We found a 3–100 fold increase in killing of the strain carrying the murA S368P allele when the strains were treated with isoniazid, meropenem or rifampin at the initiation of starvation (Figure 6D).
evidence: Experimental data from antibiotic kill curves shown in Figure 6D

claim: The murA S368P mutant had a significant antibiotic tolerance defect in nutrient rich media.
source: The mutant also had a significant antibiotic tolerance defect in nutrient rich media, but not when the antibiotics were added late in starvation (Figure 6—figure supplement 1F,G), after the period in which post-translational regulation of MurA affects PG metabolism (Figure 6C).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1F,G

claim: The PknB-CwlM-MurA signaling cascade functions to quickly turn off PG synthesis during nutrient restriction.
source: We conclude that the PknB-CwlM-MurA signaling cascade functions to quickly turn off PG synthesis during nutrient restriction (Figure 7), and that this regulation contributes to antibiotic tolerance during growth and under changing conditions.
evidence: Inferred from all experimental data and summarized in Figure 7

claim: Regulation of PG biosynthesis contributes to antibiotic tolerance during growth and under changing conditions.
source: We conclude that the PknB-CwlM-MurA signaling cascade functions to quickly turn off PG synthesis during nutrient restriction (Figure 7), and that this regulation contributes to antibiotic tolerance during growth and under changing conditions.
evidence: Inferred from antibiotic sensitivity experiments

claim: All actinobacterial cwlM homologues lack secretion signals.
source: We found that all actinobacterial cwlM homologues lack secretion signals.
evidence: Bioinformatic analysis of cwlM homologues

claim: Potential phosphorylation motifs are conserved in most clades of actinobacterial cwlM homologues, irrespective of whether or not they conserve the canonical Zn2+-coordinating residues.
source: Potential phosphorylation motifs are conserved in most clades, irrespective of whether or not they conserve the canonical Zn2+-coordinating residues.
evidence: Bioinformatic analysis of cwlM homologues

claim: Both CwlM cytoplasmic localization and regulation by phosphorylation were present in an ancestor of the Actinobacteria.
source: These data imply that both CwlM cytoplasmic localization and, possibly, regulation by phosphorylation were present in an ancestor of the Actinobacteria.
evidence: Inferred from phylogenetic analysis

claim: CwlM is located in the cytoplasm.
source: We find that CwlM is located in the cytoplasm, is phosphorylated by the essential Serine Threonine Protein Kinase (STPK) PknB, and functions to stimulate the catalytic activity of MurA, the first enzyme in the PG precursor synthesis pathway.
evidence: Experimental data from SCAM assay

claim: CwlM is phosphorylated by the essential Serine Threonine Protein Kinase (STPK) PknB.
source: We find that CwlM is located in the cytoplasm, is phosphorylated by the essential Serine Threonine Protein Kinase (STPK) PknB, and functions to stimulate the catalytic activity of MurA, the first enzyme in the PG precursor synthesis pathway.
evidence: Experimental data from in vitro and in vivo phosphorylation assays

claim: CwlM functions to stimulate the catalytic activity of MurA.
source: We find that CwlM is located in the cytoplasm, is phosphorylated by the essential Serine Threonine Protein Kinase (STPK) PknB, and functions to stimulate the catalytic activity of MurA, the first enzyme in the PG precursor synthesis pathway.
evidence: Experimental data from MurA kinetic assays

claim: In nutrient-replete conditions CwlM is phosphorylated.
source: In nutrient-replete conditions CwlM is phosphorylated.
evidence: Experimental data from immunoprecipitation and western blot

claim: Phosphorylated CwlM (CwlM~P) increases the rate of MurA catalysis by ~30 fold.
source: Using in vitro biochemistry we show that phosphorylated CwlM (CwlM~P) increases the rate of MurA catalysis by ~30 fold.
evidence: Experimental data from MurA kinetic assays

claim: In starvation, CwlM is dephosphorylated and in this state does not activate MurA.
source: In starvation, CwlM is dephosphorylated and in this state does not activate MurA, which has very low activity alone (Xu et al., 2014).
evidence: Experimental data from immunoprecipitation and western blot, and cited from external source (Xu et al., 2014)

claim: Over-activation of MurA in the transition to starvation causes increased sensitivity to multiple classes of antibiotics.
source: Importantly, we find that over-activation of MurA in the transition to starvation causes increased sensitivity to multiple classes of antibiotics.
evidence: Experimental data from antibiotic kill curves

claim: CwlM protein evolution was driven by localization to the cytoplasm.
source: Finally, a phylogenetic analysis implies that CwlM protein evolution was driven by localization to the cytoplasm.
evidence: Inferred from phylogenetic analysis

claim: CwlM coordinates peptidoglycan synthesis with nutrient availability.
source: We found that CwlM, a protein homologous to peptidoglycan amidases, coordinates peptidoglycan synthesis with nutrient availability.
evidence: Inferred from all experimental data showing CwlM phosphorylation changes with nutrient availability and affects MurA activity

claim: CwlM is sequestered from peptidoglycan (PG) by localization in the cytoplasm.
source: Surprisingly, CwlM is sequestered from peptidoglycan (PG) by localization in the cytoplasm, and its enzymatic function is not essential.
evidence: Experimental data from SCAM assay and complementation with amidase-ablated mutant

claim: CwlM's enzymatic function is not essential.
source: Surprisingly, CwlM is sequestered from peptidoglycan (PG) by localization in the cytoplasm, and its enzymatic function is not essential.
evidence: Experimental data showing amidase-ablated mutant can complement WT

claim: CwlM associates with MurA.
source: Rather, CwlM is phosphorylated and associates with MurA, the first enzyme in PG precursor synthesis.
evidence: Experimental data from co-immunoprecipitation

claim: Phosphorylated CwlM activates MurA ~30 fold.
source: Phosphorylated CwlM activates MurA ~30 fold.
evidence: Experimental data from MurA kinetic assays

claim: CwlM dephosphorylation in starvation results in lower MurA activity, decreased cell wall metabolism, and increased tolerance to multiple antibiotics.
source: CwlM is dephosphorylated in starvation, resulting in lower MurA activity, decreased cell wall metabolism, and increased tolerance to multiple antibiotics.
evidence: Experimental data from phosphorylation assays, TADA staining, and antibiotic kill curves

claim: Localization in the cytoplasm drove the evolution of CwlM.
source: A phylogenetic analysis of cwlM implies that localization in the cytoplasm drove the evolution of this factor.
evidence: Inferred from phylogenetic analysis

claim: The system that controls cell wall metabolism in response to starvation contributes to antibiotic tolerance.
source: We describe a system that controls cell wall metabolism in response to starvation, and show that this regulation contributes to antibiotic tolerance.
evidence: Experimental data from antibiotic kill curves
